325	### Manual filtering: file types
326	
327	Over time, you might notice that you use the same glob patterns over and over.
328	For example, you might find yourself doing a lot of searches where you only
329	want to see results for Rust files:
330	
331	```
332	$ rg 'fn run' -g '*.rs'
333	```
334	
335	Instead of writing out the glob every time, you can use ripgrep's support for
336	file types:
337	
338	```
339	$ rg 'fn run' --type rust
340	```
341	
342	or, more succinctly,
343	
344	```
345	$ rg 'fn run' -trust
346	```
347	
348	The way the `--type` flag functions is simple. It acts as a name that is
349	assigned to one or more globs that match the relevant files. This lets you
350	write a single type that might encompass a broad range of file extensions. For
351	example, if you wanted to search C files, you'd have to check both C source
352	files and C header files:
353	
354	```
355	$ rg 'int main' -g '*.{c,h}'
356	```
357	
358	or you could just use the C file type:
359	
360	```
361	$ rg 'int main' -tc
362	```
363	
364	Just as you can write blacklist globs, you can blacklist file types too:
365	
366	```
367	$ rg clap --type-not rust
368	```
369	
370	or, more succinctly,
371	
372	```
373	$ rg clap -Trust
374	```
375	
376	That is, `-t` means "include files of this type" where as `-T` means "exclude
377	files of this type."
378	
379	To see the globs that make up a type, run `rg --type-list`:
380	
381	```
382	$ rg --type-list | rg '^make:'
383	make: *.mak, *.mk, GNUmakefile, Gnumakefile, Makefile, gnumakefile, makefile
384	```
385	
386	By default, ripgrep comes with a bunch of pre-defined types. Generally, these
387	types correspond to well known public formats. But you can define your own
388	types as well. For example, perhaps you frequently search "web" files, which
389	consist of JavaScript, HTML and CSS:
390	
391	```
392	$ rg --type-add 'web:*.html' --type-add 'web:*.css' --type-add 'web:*.js' -tweb title
393	```
394	
395	or, more succinctly,
396	
397	```
398	$ rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' -tweb title
399	```
400	
401	The above command defines a new type, `web`, corresponding to the glob
402	`*.{html,css,js}`. It then applies the new filter with `-tweb` and searches for
403	the pattern `title`. If you ran
404	
405	```
406	$ rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' --type-list
407	```
408	
409	Then you would see your `web` type show up in the list, even though it is not
410	part of ripgrep's built-in types.
411	
412	It is important to stress here that the `--type-add` flag only applies to the
413	current command. It does not add a new file type and save it somewhere in a
414	persistent form. If you want a type to be available in every ripgrep command,
415	then you should either create a shell alias:
416	
417	```
418	alias rg="rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}'"
419	```
420	
421	or add `--type-add=web:*.{html,css,js}` to your ripgrep configuration file.
422	([Configuration files](#configuration-file) are covered in more detail later.)
423	
424	#### The special `all` file type
425	
426	A special option supported by the `--type` flag is `all`. `--type all` looks
427	for a match in any of the supported file types listed by `--type-list`,
428	including those added on the command line using `--type-add`. It's equivalent
429	to the command `rg --type agda --type asciidoc --type asm ...`, where `...`
430	stands for a list of `--type` flags for the rest of the types in `--type-list`.
431	
432	As an example, let's suppose you have a shell script in your current directory,
433	`my-shell-script`, which includes a shell library, `my-shell-library.bash`.
434	Both `rg --type sh` and `rg --type all` would only search for matches in
435	`my-shell-library.bash`, not `my-shell-script`, because the globs matched
436	by the `sh` file type don't include files without an extension. On the
437	other hand, `rg --type-not all` would search `my-shell-script` but not
438	`my-shell-library.bash`.

541	### Configuration file
542	
543	It is possible that ripgrep's default options aren't suitable in every case.
544	For that reason, and because shell aliases aren't always convenient, ripgrep
545	supports configuration files.
546	
547	Setting up a configuration file is simple. ripgrep will not look in any
548	predetermined directory for a config file automatically. Instead, you need to
549	set the `RIPGREP_CONFIG_PATH` environment variable to the file path of your
550	config file. Once the environment variable is set, open the file and just type
551	in the flags you want set automatically. There are only two rules for
552	describing the format of the config file:
553	
554	1. Every line is a shell argument, after trimming whitespace.
555	2. Lines starting with `#` (optionally preceded by any amount of whitespace)
556	are ignored.
557	
558	In particular, there is no escaping. Each line is given to ripgrep as a single
559	command line argument verbatim.
560	
561	Here's an example of a configuration file, which demonstrates some of the
562	formatting peculiarities:
563	
564	```
565	$ cat $HOME/.ripgreprc
566	# Don't let ripgrep vomit really long lines to my terminal, and show a preview.
567	--max-columns=150
568	--max-columns-preview
569	
570	# Add my 'web' type.
571	--type-add
572	web:*.{html,css,js}*
573	
574	# Search hidden files / directories (e.g. dotfiles) by default
575	--hidden
576	
577	# Using glob patterns to include/exclude files or folders
578	--glob=!.git/*

{"file_path":"<path>","content":"# Filtering ripgrep searches by file type

If you search text for a living, you already reach for globs (`-g '*.rs'`) to
keep noise out of your results. ripgrep's file-type flags do the same job
without you having to remember or retype extension lists: `--type`,
`--type-not`, `--type-add`, and `--type-list` let you say "only Rust files" or
"skip anything that's a lockfile" using a short, memorable name instead.

## The four flags at a glance

- `-t`/`--type TYPE` — only search files matching `TYPE`.
- `-T`/`--type-not TYPE` — do not search files matching `TYPE`.
- `--type-add TYPESPEC` — define (or extend) a type for the current command.
- `--type-list` — print every type ripgrep knows about, along with the globs
  behind it.

Under the hood, a "type" is just a name bound to one or more glob patterns.
`--type rust` is shorthand for `-g '*.rs'`; it saves you from remembering the
glob and from having to write it out for types that cover several extensions,
like C, which needs both `*.c` and `*.h`.

## `--type`: search only matching files

```
$ rg 'fn run' --type rust
$ rg 'fn run' -trust        # short flag, value glued on
```

Multiple `--type` flags can be given, and they combine additively — each adds
more files to the search rather than narrowing it further. This is also how
`-t` differs from a glob you write yourself: it's a name for "one or more
globs that match the relevant files," which is why a single type can stand in
for a whole family of extensions. For instance, ripgrep's built-in `c` type
covers `*.[chH]`, `*.[chH].in`, and `*.cats` in one name, and `make` covers
eight different filename patterns (`Makefile`, `GNUmakefile`, `*.mk`, `*.mak`,
and their case variants) so you don't have to enumerate them with `-g`.

`--type` also accepts the special value `all`, which behaves as though you'd
passed `--type` for every file type ripgrep knows, including any you defined
yourself with `--type-add`. This puts ripgrep into a "whitelist" mode: it
searches only files it recognizes via its type definitions, and skips
extensionless or otherwise unrecognized files. A shell script named
`my-shell-script` (no extension) is *not* matched by the `sh` type's globs, so
neither `--type sh` nor `--type all` would search it — only a file like
`my-shell-library.bash` would.

One subtlety worth knowing: `--type` has lower precedence than both `--glob`
and any rules in your ignore files. If a `.gitignore` or an explicit `-g`
excludes a file, `--type` won't override that exclusion.

## `--type-not`: exclude matching files

`--type-not` (short form `-T`) is the mirror image of `--type` — everything
that would normally be searched is searched *except* files of the given
type:

```
$ rg clap --type-not rust
$ rg clap -Trust
```

As the project's own guide puts it: `-t` means "include files of this type,"
whereas `-T` means "exclude files of this type." You can mix both in one
command — for example `-Trust -ttoml -Tjson` negates `rust` and `json` while
selecting `toml`.

`--type-not` also understands `all`. `--type-not all` flips the whitelist
logic from `--type all` into a "blacklist" for *unrecognized* files: it
searches only files that ripgrep's type definitions don't recognize. Using
the earlier example, `--type-not all` would search `my-shell-script` (no
recognized extension) but skip `my-shell-library.bash` (recognized by the
`sh` type).

## `--type-add`: define your own types

ripgrep ships with a large set of built-in types (on the order of 200 names,
covering everything from `agda` to `zig`), but you'll inevitably want one it
doesn't have — or a grouping that spans several existing types. `--type-add`
takes a `TYPESPEC` of the form `name:glob` and adds that glob to the named
type, creating the type if it doesn't already exist. Only one glob can be
added per flag, but you can repeat the flag:

```
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.html' --type-add 'web:*.css' --type-add 'web:*.js' -tweb title
```

or, using brace expansion in the glob to do it in one flag:

```
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' -tweb title
```

Both create a new `web` type matching HTML, CSS, and JS files, then search it
for `title`. Type names may only contain Unicode letters or numbers — no
punctuation.

`--type-add` also supports an `include:` directive that pulls in the globs
from other, already-defined types, which is handy for building composite
types out of existing ones:

```
$ rg --type-add 'src:include:cpp,py,md' PATTERN
```

You can still add more globs to `src` afterward with another `--type-add`.
Pair this with `--type-clear TYPE` if you want to strip a built-in type's
existing globs before adding your own instead of extending them.

The important caveat: `--type-add` is not persistent. It only affects the
current invocation — ripgrep doesn't remember your `web` type for next time.
To make a custom type available everywhere, either alias it in your shell:

```
alias rg="rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}'"
```

or add it to a ripgrep configuration file (pointed to by the
`RIPGREP_CONFIG_PATH` environment variable), one flag and value per line:

```
--type-add
web:*.{html,css,js}
```

## `--type-list`: see what's available

`--type-list` prints every type ripgrep currently knows — built-in types plus
anything you've added with `--type-add` (and minus anything removed with
`--type-clear`) — one per line, as `name: glob, glob, ...`:

```
$ rg --type-list | rg '^make:'
make: *.mak, *.mk, GNUmakefile, Gnumakefile, Makefile, gnumakefile, makefile
```

This is the fastest way to check whether a type you're about to pass to
`-t`/`-T` actually exists, and exactly which files it will pull in — useful
before you commit to `--type-add`ing a duplicate, or before you rely on
`--type all` / `--type-not all` and want to know what counts as "recognized."
Running it after a `--type-add` also confirms your custom type registered
correctly, since it will show up in the output even though it isn't one of
ripgrep's built-ins.

## Putting it together

A typical workflow: run `rg --type-list` once to learn the name for the
language or format you care about (or confirm none exists), use `-t`/`-T` day
to day instead of hand-written globs, and reach for `--type-add` — backed by
a shell alias or config file entry — when you have a recurring, project- or
team-specific grouping (like the `web` example) that isn't worth retyping as
a glob every time.
"}

62	whereas `-T` means "exclude files of this type." You can mix both in one
63	command — for example `-Trust -ttoml -Tjson` negates `rust` and `json` while
64	selecting `toml`.
65	
66	`--type-not` also understands `all`. `--type-not all` flips the whitelist
67	logic from `--type all` into a "blacklist" for *unrecognized* files: it
68	searches only files that ripgrep's type definitions don't recognize. Using
69	the earlier example, `--type-not all` would search `my-shell-script` (no
70	recognized extension) but skip `my-shell-library.bash` (recognized by the
71	`sh` type).
72	
73	## `--type-add`: define your own types
74	
75	ripgrep ships with a large set of built-in types (on the order of 200 names,
76	covering everything from `agda` to `zig`), but you'll want one it doesn't
77	have, or a grouping that spans several existing types. `--type-add` takes a
78	`TYPESPEC` of the form `name:glob` and adds that glob to the named type,
79	creating the type if it doesn't already exist. Only one glob can be added per
80	flag, but you can repeat the flag:
81	
82	```
83	$ rg --type-add 'web:*.html' --type-add 'web:*.css' --type-add 'web:*.js' -tweb title
84	```
85	
86	or, using brace expansion in the glob to do it in one flag:
87	
88	```
89	$ rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' -tweb title
90	```
91	
92	Both create a new `web` type matching HTML, CSS, and JS files, then search it
93	for `title`. Type names may only contain Unicode letters or numbers — no
94	punctuation.
95	
96	`--type-add` also supports an `include:` directive that pulls in the globs
97	from other, already-defined types, which is handy for building composite
98	types out of existing ones:
99	
100	```
101	$ rg --type-add 'src:include:cpp,py,md' PATTERN
102	```
103	
104	You can still add more globs to `src` afterward with another `--type-add`.
105	Pair this with `--type-clear TYPE` if you want to strip a built-in type's
106	existing globs before adding your own instead of extending them.
107	
108	The important caveat: `--type-add` is not persistent. It only affects the
109	current invocation — ripgrep doesn't remember your `web` type for next time.
110	To make a custom type available everywhere, either alias it in your shell:
111	
112	```
113	alias rg="rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}'"
114	```
115	
116	or add it to a ripgrep configuration file (pointed to by the
117	`RIPGREP_CONFIG_PATH` environment variable), one flag and value per line:
118	
119	```
120	--type-add
121	web:*.{html,css,js}
122	```
123	
124	## `--type-list`: see what's available
125	
126	`--type-list` prints every type ripgrep currently knows — built-in types plus
127	anything you've added with `--type-add` (and minus anything removed with
128	`--type-clear`) — one per line, as `name: glob, glob, ...`:
129	
130	```
131	$ rg --type-list | rg '^make:'
132	make: *.mak, *.mk, GNUmakefile, Gnumakefile, Makefile, gnumakefile, makefile
133	```
134	
135	This is the fastest way to check whether a type you're about to pass to
136	`-t`/`-T` exists, and exactly which files it pulls in — useful before
137	`--type-add`ing a duplicate, or before relying on `--type all` /
138	`--type-not all` and wanting to know what counts as "recognized." Running it
139	after a `--type-add` also confirms your custom type registered, since it
140	shows up in the output even though it isn't a built-in.
141	
142	## Putting it together
143	
144	A typical workflow: run `rg --type-list` once to learn the name for the
145	language or format you care about (or confirm none exists), use `-t`/`-T` day
146	to day instead of hand-written globs, and reach for `--type-add` — backed by
147	a shell alias or config file entry — when you have a recurring, project- or
148	team-specific grouping (like the `web` example) that isn't worth retyping as
149	a glob every time.
150

1	# Filtering ripgrep searches by file type
2	
3	If you search text for a living, you already reach for globs (`-g '*.rs'`) to
4	keep noise out of your results. ripgrep's file-type flags do the same job
5	without retyping extension lists: `--type`, `--type-not`, `--type-add`, and
6	`--type-list` let you say "only Rust files" using a short, memorable name.
7	
8	## The four flags at a glance
9	
10	- `-t`/`--type TYPE` — only search files matching `TYPE`.
11	- `-T`/`--type-not TYPE` — do not search files matching `TYPE`.
12	- `--type-add TYPESPEC` — define (or extend) a type for the current command.
13	- `--type-list` — print every type ripgrep knows about, along with the globs
14	  behind it.
15	
16	Under the hood, a "type" is just a name bound to one or more glob patterns.
17	`--type rust` is shorthand for `-g '*.rs'`, and saves writing out the glob for
18	types that cover several extensions, like C, which needs both `*.c` and
19	`*.h`.
20	
21	## `--type`: search only matching files
22	
23	```
24	$ rg 'fn run' --type rust
25	$ rg 'fn run' -trust        # short flag, value glued on
26	```
27	
28	Multiple `--type` flags can be given, and they combine additively — each adds
29	more files to the search rather than narrowing it further. This is also how
30	`-t` differs from a glob you write yourself: it's a name for "one or more
31	globs that match the relevant files," so a single type can stand in for a
32	whole family of extensions. For instance, ripgrep's built-in `c` type covers
33	`*.[chH]`, `*.[chH].in`, and `*.cats` in one name, and `make` covers eight
34	filename patterns (`Makefile`, `GNUmakefile`, `*.mk`, `*.mak`, and case
35	variants) so you don't have to enumerate them with `-g`.
36	
37	`--type` also accepts the special value `all`, behaving as though `--type`
38	were passed for every file type ripgrep knows, including any added with
39	`--type-add`. This puts ripgrep in a "whitelist" mode: it searches only files
40	it recognizes via its type definitions, skipping extensionless or otherwise
41	unrecognized files. A shell script named `my-shell-script` (no extension)
42	isn't matched by the `sh` type's globs, so neither `--type sh` nor
43	`--type all` would search it — only a file like `my-shell-library.bash`
44	would.
45	
46	One subtlety: `--type` has lower precedence than both `--glob` and any rules
47	in your ignore files, so a `.gitignore` exclusion or an explicit `-g` wins
48	over `--type`.
49	
50	## `--type-not`: exclude matching files
51	
52	`--type-not` (short form `-T`) is the mirror image of `--type` — everything
53	that would normally be searched is searched *except* files of the given
54	type:
55	
56	```
57	$ rg clap --type-not rust
58	$ rg clap -Trust
59	```
60	
61	As the project's own guide puts it: `-t` means "include files of this type,"
62	`-T` means "exclude files of this type." You can mix both in one command —
63	`-Trust -ttoml -Tjson` negates `rust` and `json` while selecting `toml`.
64	
65	`--type-not` also understands `all`, flipping `--type all`'s whitelist into a
66	"blacklist" for *unrecognized* files: `--type-not all` would search
67	`my-shell-script` (no recognized extension) but skip
68	`my-shell-library.bash` (recognized by the `sh` type).
69	
70	## `--type-add`: define your own types
71	
72	ripgrep ships with a large set of built-in types (on the order of 200 names,
73	covering everything from `agda` to `zig`), but you'll want one it doesn't
74	have, or a grouping that spans several existing types. `--type-add` takes a
75	`TYPESPEC` of the form `name:glob` and adds that glob to the named type,
76	creating the type if it doesn't already exist. Only one glob can be added per
77	flag, but you can repeat the flag:
78	
79	```
80	$ rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' -tweb title
81	```
82	
83	This creates a new `web` type matching HTML, CSS, and JS files (brace
84	expansion lets one flag do what would otherwise take three), then searches it
85	for `title`. Type names may only contain Unicode letters or numbers — no
86	punctuation.
87	
88	`--type-add` also supports an `include:` directive that pulls in the globs
89	from other, already-defined types, useful for building composite types:
90	
91	```
92	$ rg --type-add 'src:include:cpp,py,md' PATTERN
93	```
94	
95	More globs can still be added to `src` with another `--type-add`. Pair this
96	with `--type-clear TYPE` to strip a built-in type's existing globs before
97	adding your own instead of extending them.
98	
99	The important caveat: `--type-add` is not persistent — it only affects the
100	current invocation. To make a custom type available everywhere, alias it in
101	your shell (`alias rg="rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}'"`) or add
102	`--type-add` and its value as two lines in a ripgrep configuration file
103	(pointed to by the `RIPGREP_CONFIG_PATH` environment variable).
104	
105	## `--type-list`: see what's available
106	
107	`--type-list` prints every type ripgrep currently knows — built-in types plus
108	anything you've added with `--type-add` (and minus anything removed with
109	`--type-clear`) — one per line, as `name: glob, glob, ...`:
110	
111	```
112	$ rg --type-list | rg '^make:'
113	make: *.mak, *.mk, GNUmakefile, Gnumakefile, Makefile, gnumakefile, makefile
114	```
115	
116	This is the fastest way to check whether a type you're about to pass to
117	`-t`/`-T` exists and exactly which files it pulls in — useful before
118	`--type-add`ing a duplicate, before relying on `--type all`/`--type-not all`,
119	or to confirm a custom type registered correctly.
120	
121	## Putting it together
122	
123	A typical workflow: check `rg --type-list` for the name you need, use `-t`/`-T`
124	day to day instead of hand-written globs, and reach for `--type-add` — backed
125	by a shell alias or config file entry — for recurring, project-specific
126	groupings not worth retyping as a glob every time.
